53.note: This statute supports a specific statutory aspect concerning disrespect to the Constitution; it does not codify all Fundamental Duties.

103.note: These Acts provide statutory property/acquisition context; Article 300A remains the constitutional foundation.

189.note: The Constitution supplies the service framework; these statutes provide statutory service and anti-corruption context.

191.note: Use statutory accountability laws only for their actual scope; constitutional and judicial accountability remain separately sourced.

288.note: Local-body election law is primarily state-specific; the lesson must not invent a single uniform all-India municipal or Panchayat election statute.

291.note: Electoral corrupt practices and any applicable criminal offences must be distinguished and sourced separately.

293.note: The statutory election framework contains specific provisions concerning appeals to caste and related electoral corrupt practices.

294.note: The statutory election framework contains specific provisions concerning appeals to religion and related electoral corrupt practices.

295.note: False statements in election contexts and digital communication must be treated under their respective legal frameworks; do not equate all false information with an offence.

299.note: Elections are one part of democracy; statutory election and transparency frameworks provide concrete examples without replacing constitutional principles.

334.note: The statutory right to information is governed by the Right to Information Act, 2005; Article 19(1)(a) is a constitutional foundation, not the complete statutory framework.

339.note: The cited Acts cover important statutory accountability routes, not every general government grievance mechanism.

342.note: The statutory sources must be used only for provisions that actually apply; constitutional and judicial limits on speech must be kept distinct.

93.note: Article 24 is supplemented by the statutory child-labour framework.

247.note: Lok Adalats are a statutory mechanism; Article 39A alone is not sufficient.

259.note: The Act provides the statutory framework for contempt; constitutional Articles 129 and 215 remain the constitutional foundation.

278.note: Candidate qualifications and disqualifications must be distinguished between the Constitution and election statute.

279.note: Political-party registration and election-symbol regulation are governed by the applicable election law and ECI order.

280.note: Campaign conduct must be described from applicable election law and rules; the Model Code is not treated as an Act.

281.note: Election procedures are governed by the constitutional framework, election legislation and rules.

282.note: Secrecy of voting is specifically addressed by election law and rules.

284.note: Representative elections and their conduct are governed by the constitutional and statutory election framework.

285.note: Counting and declaration of results must be described from the applicable election law and rules.

286.note: Lok Sabha elections use the statutory electoral-roll and election-conduct framework.

287.note: State Assembly elections use the statutory electoral-roll and election-conduct framework.

289.note: By-elections are governed by the applicable constitutional and election-law framework.

290.note: Election expenditure is regulated by the Representation of the People Act and Conduct of Elections Rules.

292.note: Election expenditure and corrupt-practice rules provide the statutory election-law context.

297.note: Candidate evaluation should distinguish constitutional qualifications, statutory disqualifications and election disclosures from subjective political judgments.

305.note: Detailed Sarpanch powers and duties are governed by the applicable State Panchayati Raj law; the Constitution provides the framework but not one uniform all-India Sarpanch statute.

316.note: Local grievance mechanisms vary by State and local body; the lesson must not invent one nationwide complaint procedure. RTI is a separate statutory transparency route.

318.note: Social-audit rules differ by programme and State. MGNREGA provides a specific statutory social-audit framework for works under that Act; it must not be generalized to every local project.

319.note: Local-government accountability and corruption must be described using applicable State/local laws plus the separate statutory transparency and anti-corruption frameworks.
